en: Sūtra 1: Tree I (The Tree) NidSa 1.1: The setting was Śrāvastī.
NidSa 1.2: There the Blessed One addressed the monks.

NidSa 1.3: For one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena conducive to grasping, craving increases. With craving as condition, grasping arises; with grasping as condition, existence arises.
With existence as condition, birth occurs;
with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
Thus there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.

It is just as if a man, desiring its welfare, seeking its benefit, and seeking its security and well-being, were to appear for a young, newly sprouted tree; he would from time to time loosen its roots, from time to time provide it with cold and warmth, and from time to time give it water.
That tree, on account of that, would attain growth, development, and expansion.
NidSa 1.5 In the same way, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena conducive to grasping, craving increases, as previously described, until there is origination.

NidSa 1.6 For one who dwells contemplating impermanence in phenomena conducive to grasping, contemplating their disintegration, contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation, and contemplating relinquishment, craving ceases.
From the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging;
from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence;
from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth.
From the cessation of birth comes the cessation of old age and death;
sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.

It is just as if, for example, there were a man who desired what was harmful, what was unbeneficial, and what was not conducive to security, and he would come upon that very tree— new and young— and having cut it down at its root, [he would carry it] from the top... [and so forth].
One should dry it by means of wind and sun;
having dried it by means of wind and sun, one should burn it with fire;
having burned it with fire... [it becomes] ... [the state of] ... [the ultimate reality].

“Bhikṣus, what do you think? Has not that tree, with its root cut off like the top of a palm tree, become one that has reached the end of existence and is subject to non-arising in the future? “Yes, Venerable Sir.
“In the same way, when one perceives impermanence, disintegration, fading away, cessation, and relinquishment in phenomena that are objects of clinging, craving ceases.”
From the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging;
from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of becoming;
from the cessation of becoming comes the cessation of birth.
With the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death;
sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
Then those monks rejoiced in what was spoken by the Blessed One;
having rejoiced and approved it, they departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Sūtra 2: Tree II (The Tree) NidSa 2.1: The setting was Śrāvastī.
NidSa 2.2: There the Blessed One addressed the monks.
"Monks, for one who dwells observing the gratification in phenomena conducive to clinging, consciousness becomes attracted to name-and-form.
With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise;
with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises."
Contact is the condition for feeling;
feeling is the condition for craving;
craving is the condition for clinging.
With clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises;
and with birth as condition, aging and death, along with sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, come into being.
In this way, there occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
Just as for a great tree—possessing roots, a trunk, pith, and provided with branches, leaves, and fruit—the roots that extend downward draw up nourishment toward the top;
so too, that great tree, having that as its nutriment and that as its basis, persists for a long time.

In the same way, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena that are subject to clinging, consciousness becomes a carrier toward name-and-form, and so on, as before, until there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering. (NidSa 2.5) But for one who dwells contemplating impermanence, contemplating disintegration, contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation, and contemplating relinquishment in phenomena that are subject to clinging, consciousness does not become a carrier. (NidSa 2.6)
From the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases;
from the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact.
With the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling;
with the cessation of feeling, there is the cessation of craving;
with the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging.
From the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence;
from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth;
from the cessation of birth comes the cessation of old age and death.
Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
In this way, there comes to be the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
Just as, for example, a man might appear for that very same great tree—possessing roots, a trunk, pith, and endowed with branches, leaves, and fruit—[and cut it down... NidSa 2.7.

“Bhikṣus, what do you think? Has not that great tree, with its root cut off like the top of a palmyra tree, become subject to non-becoming, having no further course in the future, and being of a nature not to arise again? “Yes, Venerable Sir.

“In the same way, for one who contemplates impermanence, disintegration, fading away, cessation, and relinquishment regarding phenomena that are objects of clinging, there is no more bringing [of suffering].”
Consciousness exists in name-and-form;
from its cessation comes the cessation of the six sense bases,
and so on, as before, until cessation occurs.
Then those monks rejoiced in the words spoken by the Blessed One;
having rejoiced and approved, they departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Sūtras 3 and 4: Dīpa I and II (The Lamp) NidSa 3.1: "Monks, before I had awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, while I was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind:
NidSa 3.2: ‘Alas, this world has fallen into hardship; that is to say, it is born, it ages, it dies, it passes away, and it is reborn.’"
And yet, these beings do not understand, as it truly is, the escape beyond aging and death.
Then this occurred to me:
"When what exists does aging and death come to be?"
And what is the condition for old age and death?
As I reflected thoroughly upon this, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are:
when birth exists, old age and death come to be.
And furthermore, conditioned by birth, there is aging and death.
Then this occurred to me:
"What being present does birth come to be?"
And what is the condition for birth?
As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me this realization of things as they truly are:
when existence is present, birth comes to be.
Furthermore, birth has existence as its condition.
Then this occurred to me:
"When what exists does existence come to be?"
And what is the condition for renewed existence?
As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me this realization of things as they truly are:
when there is grasping, there is existence.
"And furthermore, conditioned by grasping (upādāna) is renewed existence (bhava).
Then this occurred to me:
'In what being present does grasping come to be?'"
"And what is the condition for grasping?
As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me this realization of reality as it is:
"For one who dwells perceiving gratification in phenomena that lead to grasping, craving increases."
With craving as condition, grasping arises;
with grasping as condition, becoming arises;
with becoming as condition, birth arises.
With birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
What do you think, monks? ... [NidSa 3.7]
"Yes, Venerable Sir.
"In the same way, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena that are objects of clinging, craving increases; with craving as condition, there is clinging;
with clinging as condition, there is existence."
With existence as condition, birth occurs;
with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
Then this occurred to me:
"In what being absent do aging and death not come to be?
Through the cessation of what does the cessation of aging and death occur?"
As I applied my mind thoroughly in this way, there arose in me a realization of reality as it is:
when birth does not exist, aging and death do not occur;
with the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death.
Then this occurred to me:
"In what being absent does birth not come to be?
From the cessation of what does the cessation of birth occur?"
As I was attending to this thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me a realization of reality as it is: "When existence does not exist, birth does not come to be;
from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth.
Then this occurred to me: *NidSa* 3.12.
"When what does not exist does existence not come to be?
From the cessation of what does the cessation of existence occur?
As I applied my mind to this with thorough attention, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are.
When there is no grasping, existence does not come to be;
from the cessation of grasping comes the cessation of existence.
(NidSa 3.13) This thought occurred to me:
"In what being absent does grasping not come to be?
From the cessation of what does the cessation of grasping occur?
As I reflected thoroughly in this way, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are.
When one contemplates the phenomena subject to clinging as impermanent, as subject to destruction, as subject to dispassion, as subject to cessation, and as subject to relinquishment, craving ceases.
From the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging;
from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence.
From the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; from the cessation of birth comes the cessation of old age and death;
sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
"Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
What do you think, monks? ... 'So it is, Blessed One.'"

In the same way, when one observes conditioned phenomena that are subject to grasping as impermanent, as subject to destruction, as subject to dispassion, as subject to cessation, and as subject to relinquishment, craving ceases.
With the cessation of craving, grasping ceases;
[and so on] as before, until there is total cessation.
Then those monks rejoiced in the words spoken by the Blessed One;
having rejoiced and approved them, they departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Sūtra 4:
NidSa 4.1. Monks, formerly, before I had awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, while I was alone and in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind:
NidSa 4.2. "Alas, this world has fallen into hardship; that is to say, it is born, it grows old, it dies, it passes away, and it is reborn."
And yet, these beings do not understand, as it truly is, the escape from beyond aging and death.
Then this occurred to me:
"When what exists does aging and death come to be?"
And what is the condition for aging and death?
As I applied my mind to this thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me a realization of reality as it is:
when birth exists, aging and death come to be.
And furthermore, old age and death have birth as their condition.
Then this occurred to me:
"When what exists does birth come to be?"
"And what is the condition for birth?
As I reflected thoroughly upon this, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are:
"When existence is present, birth comes to be."
And furthermore, birth has existence as its condition.
Then this occurred to me:
"What being present does existence come to be?"
And what is the condition for renewed existence?
As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me this realization of things as they truly are:
when there is grasping, there is existence.
And furthermore, there is becoming conditioned by clinging.
Then this occurred to me:
"Now, when what exists does clinging come to be?"
"And what, again, is the condition for clinging?
As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me this realization of things as they truly are:
"For one who dwells perceiving gratification in phenomena that lead to clinging, craving increases."
With craving as condition, grasping arises;
with grasping as condition, becoming arises;
with becoming as condition, birth arises.
With birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering. What do you think, monks? ...
“Yes, Venerable Sir.
“In the same way, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena conducive to clinging, craving increases; with craving as condition, there is clinging;
with clinging as condition, there is existence.”
With existence as condition, birth arises;
with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
This thought occurred to me:
"In what being absent do aging and death not come to be?
From the cessation of what does the cessation of aging and death result?"
As I applied my mind thoroughly in this way, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are:
when birth does not exist, aging and death do not come to be;
with the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death.
Then this occurred to me:
"In what being absent does birth not come to be?
From the cessation of what does the cessation of birth occur?"
As I was reflecting thoroughly in this way, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are: "When existence does not exist, birth does not occur;
from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth.
Then this occurred to me: *NidSa* 4.12.
"When what does not exist does existence not come to be?
From the cessation of what does the cessation of existence occur?
As I applied my mind to this with systematic attention, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are.
"When there is no grasping, existence does not come to be;
from the cessation of grasping comes the cessation of existence.
(NidSa 4.13) This thought occurred to me:
"In what being absent does grasping not come to be?
From the cessation of what does the cessation of grasping occur?
As I reflected thoroughly in this way, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are.
When one contemplates impermanence, disintegration, dispassion, cessation, and relinquishment regarding phenomena that are subject to clinging, craving ceases.
From the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging;
from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence.
From the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; from the cessation of birth comes the cessation of old age and death;
sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
"In this way, there is the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
What do you think, monks? ... "—“So it is, Blessed One.”"
In the same way, when one observes conditioned phenomena that are subject to clinging as impermanent, as disintegrating, as fading away, as ceasing, and as relinquishing, craving ceases.
From the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging,
and so on, as before, until there is cessation.
Then those monks rejoiced in the words spoken by the Blessed One;
having rejoiced and approved them, they departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Sūtra 5: The Discourse on the City (Nagarasūtra). NidSa 5.1: Success! Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, formerly, before I had awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, while I was alone, withdrawn in seclusion, and dwelling in meditative retreat, this reflection arose in my mind:
'Alas, this world has fallen into hardship; that is to say, it is born, it grows old, it dies, it passes away, and it is reborn.'"
"And yet, these beings do not understand, as it truly is, the escape beyond aging and death.
Then this occurred to me:
'When what exists does aging and death come to be?'"
And what is the condition for old age and death?
As I reflected thoroughly upon this, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are:
when birth exists, old age and death come to be.
And furthermore, with birth as condition, there is old age and death.
(NidSa 5.5) Then this occurred to me: "When what exists does birth come to be?"
"And what is the condition for birth?
As I reflected thoroughly upon this, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are:
"When existence is present, birth comes to be."
And furthermore, birth has existence as its condition.
Then this occurred to me:
"When what exists does existence come to be?"
And what is the condition for renewed existence?
As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me this realization of things as they truly are:
when there is grasping, existence comes to be.
And further, there is existence conditioned by clinging.
Then this occurred to me:
"Now, when what exists does clinging come to be?"
"And what is the condition for clinging?
As I reflected thoroughly upon this, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are:
"When craving exists, clinging comes to be."
And furthermore, craving is the condition for clinging.
Then this occurred to me:
"What being present does craving come to be?"
"And what, again, is the condition for craving?
As I applied my mind to this thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me a realization of reality as it is:
"When feeling exists, craving comes to be."
Furthermore, with feeling as condition, there is craving.
Then this occurred to me:
"What being present does feeling come to be?"
"And what is the condition for feeling?
As I applied my mind to this thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me a realization of reality as it is:
"When there is contact, feeling comes to be."
Furthermore, feeling has contact as its condition.
Then this occurred to me:
"What being present does contact come to be?"
And what is the condition for contact?
As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me this realization of things as they truly are:
when the six sense bases exist, contact comes to be.
Furthermore, with the six sense bases as condition, there is contact.
Then this occurred to me:
"When what exists do the six sense bases come to be?"
"And what is the condition for the six sense bases?
As I applied my mind thoroughly to this, there arose in me a realization of reality as it truly is:
"When name-and-form exists, the six sense bases come to be."
And furthermore, with name-and-form as condition, there are the six sense bases.
Then this occurred to me:
"What being present does name-and-form come to be?"
Furthermore, with what as its condition does name-and-form arise?
As I applied my mind to this thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me a realization of reality as it is:
when consciousness exists, name-and-form comes to be.
Furthermore, name-and-form has consciousness as its condition.
(NidSa 5.13) Then this occurred to me: "When what exists does consciousness come to be?"
"And what is the condition for consciousness?
As I applied my mind to this thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me a realization of reality as it is:
"When volitional formations exist, consciousness comes to be."
And furthermore, consciousness has volitional formations as its condition.
(NidSa 5.14) Then this occurred to me:
"Now, what being present do volitional formations come to be?"
"And what is the condition for the formative forces?
As I applied my mind to this thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are:
"When ignorance exists, the formative forces come to be."
Furthermore, "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces" (NidSa 5.15);
thus, the formative forces have ignorance as their condition.
Conditioned by the formative forces is consciousness.
Conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form;
conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases;
conditioned by the six sense bases is contact.
With contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises;
with craving as condition, clinging arises.
With clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises;
with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
"Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
(NidSa 5.16) Then this occurred to me:
"In what being absent do aging and death not come to be?"
"From the cessation of what does the cessation of old age and death occur?
As I applied my mind to this thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are:
"In the absence of birth, old age and death do not come to be."
"With the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of old age and death.
(NidSa 5.17) Then this occurred to me:
"In what being absent does birth not come to be?"
"From the cessation of what does the cessation of birth occur?
As I applied my mind to this in a systematic way, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are:
"When existence is absent, birth does not occur."
"From the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth.
(NidSa 5.18) Then this occurred to me:
"In the absence of what does existence not come to be?"
"From the cessation of what does the cessation of existence occur?
As I applied my mind to this in a systematic way, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are:
"When grasping is absent, existence does not come to be."
"With the cessation of clinging, existence ceases.
(NidSa 5.19) This occurred to me:
"In the absence of what, however, does clinging not come to be?"
"From the cessation of what does the cessation of clinging occur?
As I applied my mind to this with systematic attention, there arose in me the realization of things as they truly are:
"In the absence of craving, clinging does not come to be."
With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging.
(NidSa 5.20) This occurred to me:
"In the absence of what does craving not come to be?"
"Through the cessation of what does craving cease?
As I applied my mind to this with proper reflection, there arose in me a realization of reality as it truly is:
"In the absence of feeling, craving does not come to be."
From the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving.
At that time, this thought occurred to me:
"In what being absent does feeling not come to be?"
"From the cessation of what does the cessation of feeling occur?
As I applied my mind to this in a systematic way, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are:
"In the absence of contact, feeling does not come to be."
"With the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling.
(NidSa 5.22) This occurred to me:
"In the absence of what does contact not come to be?"
"From the cessation of what does the cessation of contact occur?
As I applied my mind to this thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me this realization of reality as it is:
"In the absence of the six sense bases, contact does not come to be."
With the cessation of the six sense bases, there is the cessation of contact.
(NidSa 5.23) This occurred to me:
"In what being absent does the sixfold sense base not come to be?"
"From the cessation of what does the cessation of the six sense bases occur?
As I applied my mind to this thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me a realization of reality as it is:
"When name-and-form is absent, the six sense bases do not come to be."
With the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the six sense bases.
(NidSa 5.24) This occurred to me:
"In the absence of what, however, does name-and-form not come to be?"
"Through the cessation of what does name-and-form cease?
As I applied my mind to this thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me a realization of reality as it is:
"When consciousness is absent, name-and-form does not come to be."
"With the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form. (NidSa 5.25) This occurred to me:
"In the absence of what does consciousness not come to be?"
"From the cessation of what does the cessation of consciousness occur?
As I applied my mind to this with thorough attention, there arose in me a realization of reality as it is:
"When volitional formations do not exist, consciousness does not come to be."
"From the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness. (NidSa 5.26) This occurred to me:
"In what being absent do volitional formations not come to be?"
"Through the cessation of what does the cessation of volitional formations occur?
As I applied my mind to this thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are:
"When ignorance is absent, volitional formations do not come to be."
From the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness.
(NidSa 5.27) Thus, from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations;
from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness.
With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases;
with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease;
with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases.
From the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling;
from the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving;
from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging.
From the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence;
from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth;
from the cessation of birth comes the cessation of old age and death.
Sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair cease;
thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering. It occurred to me: NidSa 5.28. This was my thought.
"I have discovered the ancient path, the ancient track, the ancient trail, traversed and followed by the seers of old.
Just as a man wandering through a forest thicket might discover an ancient path, an ancient track, an ancient trail, traversed and followed by men of old, and he would follow it. (NidSa 5.29)
Following it, he would see there an ancient city, an ancient royal capital, well-provided with parks, groves, and lotus ponds—splendid, well-fortified, and delightful.
It would occur to him:
"What if I were to go and inform the king?"
Then that man would inform the king thus: "May your majesty know this:
while wandering here in the forest on a slope, I saw an ancient path, an ancient track, an ancient route, traveled and followed by men of former times."
I followed after him. Following him, I saw an ancient city, an ancient royal capital, endowed with groves, endowed with lotus ponds, auspicious, well-fortified, and delightful.
May Your Majesty cause that city to be built.
NidSa 5.31 Then that king might have that city built;
and at a later time, it would become a royal capital—prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants.
NidSa 5.32 In the very same way, I have discovered the ancient path, the ancient track, the ancient trail, trodden and followed by the seers of old.
And what is that ancient path, the ancient track, the ancient trail, traversed and followed by the seers of old?
It is the noble eightfold path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
"Monks, this is the ancient path, the ancient track, the ancient trail, traveled and followed by the seers of old. I followed it;
following it, I perceived aging and death."
I saw the origin of aging and death, the cessation of aging and death, and the practice leading to the cessation of aging and death.
In the same way, I saw birth, existence, clinging, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and volitional formations;
I saw the origin of volitional formations, the cessation of volitional formations, and the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations.
NidSa 5.38: Having personally realized and directly witnessed these dharmas, I declare them to the monks;
I declare them to the nuns, to the laymen, and to the laywomen; I declare them to the various non-Buddhist ascetics, brahmins, carakas, and parivrājakas.
NidSa 5.39: In this regard, a monk who practices correctly becomes one who attains success.
One accomplishes the right method, the Dharma, and what is wholesome.
A nun, a layman, and a laywoman who practice correctly also become successful;
they accomplish the right method, the Dharma, and what is wholesome.
In this way, this holy life becomes widespread, well-established among the multitude, and fully and correctly proclaimed as far as the realms of gods and humans.

Sūtra 6: The Bundle of Reeds (Naḍakalāpika) NidSa 6.1: The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. NidSa 6.2: At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila were staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
NidSa 6.3. Then, in the evening, the venerable Śāriputra rose from his seclusion and approached the venerable Mahākauṣṭhila.
Having approached, he exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the venerable Mahākauṣṭhila and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Mahākauṣṭhila:
NidSa 6.4: “Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila, let us ask about a certain point, if you would grant the opportunity for an answer to our question. NidSa 6.5: “Ask, venerable Śāriputra.”
"Having heard it, I shall inform you.
"Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila, does aging exist? "It certainly exists, Venerable Śāriputra."
NidSa 6.6b: "Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila, is there indeed death? "There certainly is death, venerable Śāriputra.
NidSa 6.7: "Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila, is aging and death self-made?"
Is aging and death produced by another? Or is it produced both by oneself and by another? Or is it produced without being caused by either self-action or other-action?
For indeed, venerable Śāriputra, aging and death are not self-made, nor are they made by another,
nor are they both self-made and made by another.
Nor is old age and death produced without a cause, whether by one's own action or by the action of another;
rather, old age and death have birth as their condition (*jātipratyaya*).
In the same way, birth, becoming, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, and so forth are to be explained.
"Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila, is name-and-form created by itself? Or is it created by another?
Or is it both created by itself and created by another?"
"Ah! Is name-and-form produced without being caused by self-action or action by another?
For indeed, venerable Śāriputra, name-and-form is not self-made, nor is it made by another."
Name-and-form is neither self-made nor made by another, nor is it produced without a cause through neither self-action nor action by another;
rather, name-and-form has consciousness as its condition.
"Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila, is consciousness self-made? Or is it made by another?
Or is it both self-made and made by another?"
"Is consciousness perhaps produced without being caused by itself or by another?
For indeed, venerable Śāriputra, consciousness is not self-made,
nor is it made by another."
Consciousness is not self-made, nor is it made by another; nor does it arise without a cause through neither self-action nor action by another.
Rather, consciousness has name-and-form as its condition.
NidSa 6.11: "Now we understand the meaning of what the venerable Mahākauṣṭhila has said:
name-and-form is neither self-made nor made by another."
Name-and-form is neither self-made nor made by another; nor is it produced without a cause through neither self-action nor other-action.
Rather, name-and-form has consciousness as its condition.
"And yet now, we understand that consciousness has name-and-form as its condition.
Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, what indeed should be seen as the meaning of this statement? "Venerable Śāriputra, I shall therefore provide you with a simile."
For by means of a simile, some wise persons here understand the meaning of what has been said.
NidSa 6.13: It is just as if two bundles of reeds were standing upright in the air, leaning against one another;
these two stand leaning against each other.
That is to say: consciousness is conditioned by name-and-form;
name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness.
"Excellent, excellent, venerable Mahākauṣṭhila! It is exactly as it should be for a learned noble disciple who has heard the truth. *Nidānasamyukta* 6.14.

By the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila— who understood the Teacher’s instruction, was well-disciplined, confident, possessed the vision of the Deathless, and dwelt having personally realized and attained the element of the Deathless with his own body— these very profound questions were reflected upon again and again and answered with right wisdom when he was questioned.

“Those fellow religious practitioners who carry the Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila on their heads like a bundle of rags would find it a great gain and a well-obtained fortune to behold the Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila and to attend upon him. It is also a gain and a well-obtained fortune for us that we behold the Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila and attend upon him.”
NidSa 6.16: “Excellent is the discourse on the Dharma taught here by the venerable Mahākoṣṭhila!
I am able to repeat this thirty [times].

NidSa 6.17: “Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila, for the sake of revulsion toward aging and death, for dispassion, and for cessation, a monk who is a preacher of the Dharma teaches the Dharma; such a monk is indeed capable of speaking thus.”

A monk who is a preacher of the Dharma teaches the Dharma for the sake of disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding birth, existence, clinging, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, and consciousness; such a monk is capable of this discourse. A monk who is a preacher of the Dharma has set out for the sake of disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding aging and death; such a monk is capable of this discourse.

To the extent that a monk is practicing for the sake of revulsion toward consciousness, for dispassion toward it, and for its cessation—a monk who is a preacher of the Dharma is competent to speak on this.

A monk who has become perfectly liberated in mind through non-clinging regarding the outflows, for the sake of revulsion toward old age and death, for dispassion toward them, and for their cessation—a monk who is a preacher of the Dharma is competent to speak on this. [And so on] up to:

a monk who has become perfectly liberated in mind through non-clinging regarding the outflows, for the sake of revulsion toward consciousness, for dispassion toward it, and for its cessation—a monk who is a preacher of the Dharma is competent to speak on this. *Nidānasamyukta* 6.19.

"Excellent, excellent, venerable Śāriputra! It is just as it should be for a learned noble disciple who correctly understands the Teacher’s instruction, who is well-trained, confident, and has seen the Deathless.
[NidSa 6.21] As before, up to the point of their attending upon him.
[NidSa 6.22] Then, thinking, "What further remains to be done? those two good men, having rejoiced and approved of what they had said to one another, rose from their seats and departed.

Sūtra 7: The Monkey (NidSa 7.1) "Monks, an ignorant, unlearned worldling might become weary of, detached from, and liberated from this body composed of the four great elements. (NidSa 7.2) For what reason?"
"Monks, in this body composed of the four great elements, accumulation and depletion are seen, as well as taking up and laying down.

But as for that which is called 'mind' or 'mine' or 'consciousness,' it is not possible for an unlearned, ordinary person who is foolish to become disenchanted with it, detached from it, or liberated from it."
For what reason? Because for a long time this has been cherished, guarded, clung to as "mine," appropriated, and grasped by the foolish, unlearned worldling: "This is mine;
this I am."
"This is my self.
Therefore, it is not possible for an ignorant, unlearned worldling to become disenchanted with that, detached from it, or liberated from it.
Monks, it is better for an ignorant, unlearned worldling to regard this very body composed of the four great elements as the self, rather than consciousness.
For what reason?

It is observed that the body, composed of the four great elements, remains for ten years, or twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred years, or even somewhat more; it remains while being maintained. But as for that which is called "mind," or "mine," or "consciousness"—that, with the passing of various nights and days, and with the passing of moments, instants, and hours...
It proceeds in many various ways:
one thing arises as it is arising, and quite another ceases as it is ceasing.
Just as, for example, a monkey might grasp at the branch of a tree.
Having abandoned that, one would grasp another;
in the very same way, that which is called "mind," or "intellect," or "consciousness," ceases as it was previously described, as those various nights and days pass away, until it finally ceases.
In this regard, the learned noble disciple thoroughly and correctly contemplates dependent origination with wise attention:
namely, that conditioned by a contact to be experienced as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises.
Experiencing that pleasant feeling, he understands it as it really is: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling."

From the cessation of this very contact conducive to pleasant feeling, that pleasant feeling which arose in dependence upon contact conducive to pleasant feeling has ceased, it has been stilled, it has become cooled, it has gone to its end.
It is the same for [contact] conducive to painful feeling, conducive to joyful feeling, and conducive to sorrowful feeling.
Dependent upon contact to be experienced with equanimity, equanimity arises.
Being equanimous, he understands as it really is: "I experience equanimity.
Through the cessation of this very contact to be experienced with equanimity, that equanimity which arose dependent on contact to be experienced with equanimity is ceased, stilled, and become cool.
When that has subsided,
it occurs to him:
"Thus these feelings are born of contact, originate from contact, are of the same nature as contact, and arise from contact."
With the arising of this or that contact, these or those feelings arise;
with the cessation of this or that contact, these or those feelings cease, are stilled, become cooled, and come to an end.
Seeing thus, the learned noble disciple becomes weary of form, and he becomes weary of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as well.
Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate;
being dispassionate, one is liberated.
For one who is liberated, there arises the knowledge and vision: "I am liberated."
Exhausted is birth for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been done; I know no further state of existence beyond this.
Sūtra 8: Two Pieces of Wood (Dvayaṃ kāṣṭhe) NidSa 8.1 This very sutra should be recited in full, up until: "they cease, they subside, they become cooled, they pass away.
NidSa 8.2 It is just as when fire is produced and heat appears from the friction, the coming together, and the conjunction of two pieces of wood.
Then, through the separation and disjunction of those very two pieces of wood, whatever heat there was would vanish and the two pieces of wood would become cold.
In the same way, it occurs to him:
"Thus these feelings are born of contact, originate from contact, are of the nature of contact, and arise from contact."
With the arising of this or that contact, those respective feelings arise;
with the cessation of this or that contact, those respective feelings cease, become stilled, grow cool, and come to an end.
Seeing thus, the learned noble disciple is fully liberated even from contact. (NidSa 8.4)
One is liberated from feeling, perception, mental formations, and even consciousness;
one is liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.
I say that one is liberated from suffering.
Sūtra 9: The Bell-Metal Bowl (Kāṃsī) NidSa 9.1 There the Blessed One addressed the monks:
NidSa 9.2 "Examine, you all, that which has been taught by me as the internal examination."
NidSa 9.3 Then a certain monk, rising from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
NidSa 9.4 "I, however, understand this internal reflection taught by the Blessed One. NidSa 9.5 "... [he] does not satisfy [the questioner] with that answer to the question..."
At that time... In the past as well, whatever ascetics or brahmins perceived whatever in the world was pleasant and agreeable as permanent,
as stable, as secure, as healthy, as self, or as belonging to a self— they increased their craving.
Those who increased craving increased the basis of existence (*upadhi*);
those who increased the basis of existence increased suffering;
and those who increased suffering were thereby liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.
"I say that they are not liberated from suffering.
However, those ascetics or brahmins who have perceived whatever in the world is pleasant and agreeable as a disease,
as an abscess, as a thorn, as an evil, as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self— they have abandoned craving."
Those who have abandoned craving have abandoned the substratum of existence;
those who have abandoned the substratum of existence have abandoned suffering; they are fully liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.
I declare that they are fully liberated from suffering.

"Furthermore, in the future time, whatever ascetics or brahmins there may be who regard whatever in the world is pleasant and agreeable as being permanent— [regarding it] from the perspective of a tumor, a thorn, a calamity, and as impermanent— "
Viewing things as permanent, secure, healthy, as self, and as belonging to a self, they will increase craving;
those who increase craving will increase the basis for existence (*upadhi*);
those who increase the basis for existence will increase suffering.
Those who will increase suffering will not be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair;
I say they will not be liberated from suffering.
But whatever ascetics or brahmins there may be who perceive that which is pleasant and agreeable in the world as being like a disease—
They will contemplate craving as a tumor, as a thorn, as evil, as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self; they will abandon craving.
Those who abandon craving will abandon the substrata of existence;
those who abandon the substrata of existence will abandon suffering.
Those who will abandon suffering will be fully liberated from birth, old age, disease, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair;
they will be fully liberated from suffering—so I say.
{From the perspective of a tumor, from the perspective of a thorn, from the perspective of a disease, from the perspective of impermanence} Sūtra 10: The Pitcher (Kumbha).
NidSa 10.1: To what extent, monks, should a monk, when investigating thoroughly, investigate for the sake of the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering?
“Venerable sir, the teachings have the Blessed One as their root,” and so on as before, up to “I shall speak.
“NidSa 10.3a: A monk, investigating thoroughly, investigates for the sake of the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering.
If, in this regard, various kinds of suffering were to arise for sentient beings, they would arise in many and manifold ways.”
"What is the cause of this suffering? What is its origin? Of what nature is it? From what does it arise?
Examining it in this way, he understands:
"This suffering has acquisition as its cause, acquisition as its origin, acquisition as its nature, and acquisition as its source."

If the substrate (*upadhi*) were to cease entirely, in every way, completely, and without remainder; if that which is superimposed were to go to total destruction, exhaustion, and termination, then his suffering too would cease.
He understands, as it truly is, the practice leading to the cessation of suffering;
and having practiced accordingly, he becomes a follower of the Dharma.
This is called a monk who has set out for the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering, that is, for the cessation of the substrata of existence (*upadhi*).
Furthermore, a monk, while investigating thoroughly, investigates for the sake of the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering:
"What is the cause of the substrata of existence? What is their origin? Of what nature are they? From what do they arise?"
Investigating in this way, he understands:
"Basis-of-existence has craving as its source, craving as its origin, craving as its birth, craving as its production.
If craving were to cease entirely, in every way, completely and without remainder, and were to reach total disappearance, destruction, and exhaustion, then his basis-of-existence would also cease."
He understands, as it truly is, that practice which leads to the cessation of the substrata of existence;
and practicing accordingly, he becomes a follower of the Dharma.
This monk is said to be one who has set out for the complete destruction of suffering and the making of an end to suffering, namely, for the cessation of craving.
Furthermore, another monk, investigating thoroughly, investigates for the sake of the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering:
"What is the cause of craving? What is its origin? Of what nature is it? From what does it arise?
Investigating in this way, he understands.
Craving has feeling as its source, feeling as its origin, feeling as its birth, and feeling as its cause.
If feeling were to cease entirely, in every way, completely and without remainder, and were to go to total disappearance, dissolution, and exhaustion, then his craving would also cease.
He understands, as it truly is, that path which leads to the cessation of craving.
And having practiced in such a way, he becomes a follower of the Dharma.
This is called a monk who has set out for the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering, namely, for the cessation of feeling.
Furthermore, a monk, while investigating thoroughly, investigates thoroughly for the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering.
Furthermore, what is the cause of feeling? What is its origin? What is its birth? What is its source?
Examining it in this way, he understands:
Feeling has contact as its cause, contact as its origin, contact as its birth, and contact as its source.
If contact were to cease entirely, in every way, completely and without remainder, and were to reach total extinction, complete destruction, and utter exhaustion, then his feeling would also cease.
He understands, as it truly is, that path leading to the cessation of feeling;
and practicing accordingly, he becomes one who lives in accordance with the Dharma.
This is called a monk who has set out for the right destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering, namely, for the cessation of contact.
Furthermore, a monk, while investigating thoroughly, investigates thoroughly for the right destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering:
"What is the cause of contact? What is its origin? Of what nature is it? From what does it arise?"
Investigating in this way, he understands:
"Contact has the six sense bases as its cause, the six sense bases as its origin, the six sense bases as its source, and the six sense bases as its basis.

If the six sense bases were to cease entirely, in every way, completely and without remainder; if they were to be eliminated, destroyed, and brought to total exhaustion, then contact would also cease for him."
He understands, as it truly is, that practice which leads to the cessation of contact;
and being thus practiced, he becomes a follower of the Dharma.
This monk is said to be one who has set out for the right destruction of suffering and for making an end of suffering, namely, for the cessation of the six sense bases.
Furthermore, monks, a monk, investigating thoroughly, investigates for the sake of the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering:
"What is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, and what is the provenance of the six sense bases?
Investigating in this way, he understands.
The six sense bases have name-and-form as their source, name-and-form as their origin, name-and-form as their birth, and name-and-form as their cause.

If name-and-form were to cease entirely, in every way, completely and without remainder—were it to be cast off, utterly exhausted, and brought to an end—then for him the six sense bases would also cease.
He understands, as it truly is, that path which leads to the cessation of the six sense bases.
And thus practicing, he becomes a follower of the Dharma;
this is called a monk who has set out for the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end of suffering, namely, for the cessation of name-and-form.
Furthermore, a monk, while investigating thoroughly, investigates thoroughly for the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end of suffering.
Furthermore, what is the cause of name-and-form? What is its origin? Of what nature is it? From what does it arise?
Examining this thoroughly, he understands:
name-and-form has consciousness as its cause, consciousness as its origin, consciousness as its nature, and consciousness as that from which it arises.

If consciousness were to cease entirely, in every way, and in its entirety—without remainder, having reached total dissolution, exhaustion, and termination—then his name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) would also cease.
He understands, as it truly is, that path leading to the cessation of name-and-form;
and practicing accordingly, he becomes one who lives in accordance with the Dharma.
This is called a monk who has set out for the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering, namely, for the cessation of consciousness.
Furthermore, a monk, investigating thoroughly, investigates thoroughly for the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering:
"What is the cause of consciousness? What is its origin? From what is it born? What is its source?"
Investigating in this way,
he understands that consciousness has its origin in volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), is of the nature of volitional formations, and arises from volitional formations.
He performs meritorious volitional formations.
His consciousness also tends toward merit;
he performs non-meritorious volitional formations,
and his consciousness also tends toward non-merit.
He performs immovable formative activities (*abhisaṃskāra*),
and his consciousness also approaches the immovable.
By this very method, it should be understood that consciousness too has formative activity as its cause, its origin, its nature, and its source.

If all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) were to cease entirely, in every way, completely and without remainder; if they were to go to total extinction, complete destruction, and utter exhaustion; then his consciousness (*vijñāna*) would also cease.
He understands, as it truly is, that path leading to the cessation of consciousness;
and having practiced accordingly, he becomes one who lives in accordance with the Dharma.
This is called a monk who has set out for the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering, that is to say, for the cessation of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).

Furthermore, a monk, while thoroughly investigating, investigates for the sake of the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering: "What is the cause of the formative forces? What is their origin? What is their birth? What is their source? *NidSa* 10.11a.
Investigating in this way, he understands:
"Formations have ignorance as their source, ignorance as their origin, ignorance as their birth, and ignorance as their cause.
He performs meritorious formations conditioned by ignorance.
One performs even non-meritorious, immovable, and formative volitional formations conditioned by ignorance.

Therefore, it should be understood by this very method that the volitional formations have ignorance as their source, ignorance as their origin, ignorance as their birth, and ignorance as their cause.

If ignorance were to cease entirely, in every way, completely and without remainder—reaching its total disappearance, exhaustion, and termination—then for such a person, the volitional formations would also cease.
He understands, as it truly is, that path which leads to the cessation of volitional formations;
and practicing accordingly, he becomes a follower of the Dharma.
This monk is said to be one who has set out for the complete destruction of suffering and the making of an end to suffering, namely, for the cessation of ignorance.
"What do you think, monks? Would a monk for whom ignorance has faded away and true knowledge has arisen ever again perform meritorious volitional formations conditioned by ignorance,
or even perform non-meritorious or imperturbable volitional formations conditioned by ignorance?"
"No, Venerable Sir.
And why is that?
Because for the learned noble disciple, ignorance has faded away and true knowledge has arisen; through the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations."
"From the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness," and so on, as before, until "there is cessation. "Excellent, excellent, monks!
I speak thus, and you understand it thus."
Just as through the arising of this or that dharma, this or that dharma arises;
and through the cessation of this or that dharma, this or that dharma ceases, becomes stilled, becomes cooled, and passes away.
And when, for the learned noble disciple, ignorance has faded away and true knowledge has arisen... *Nidānasamyukta* 10.15.

Experiencing a sensation that has the body as its limit, he understands, as it truly is: "I am experiencing a sensation that has the body as its limit. Experiencing a sensation that has life as its limit, he understands, as it truly is: "I am experiencing a sensation that has life as its limit. And after the breaking up of the body, upon the exhaustion of life, all his sensations cease here and now without remainder.
They go to complete exhaustion, total destruction, and utter disappearance.
Just as if a strong man were to take a hot pot from a hot potter’s kiln and set it down on a level stretch of ground; its heat would vanish and the shards would become cold.

In the same way, when ignorance has faded away and knowledge has arisen for a monk, he experiences a sensation that ends with the body and understands, as it truly is, "I experience a sensation that ends with the body," and so on, as previously described, until they reach complete exhaustion and total termination.
Sūtra 11: If one should say—NidSa 11.1: A monk might say, "My doubts have been crossed over; my hesitations have vanished;
the thorn of views has been pulled out from me."
[The text] "so" (thus) [is followed by] "nameti" and then "pratyudāvartate"; cf.
SWTF s.v. pratyudāvṛt. My mind does not turn back on account of distress.
For how could there be a self for me?

NidSa 11.2: While this monk was being addressed with a discourse that is Dharma-based, noble, and supramundane—namely, "When this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises"—that is to say, "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise," and so on as before, up until "there is both origination and cessation."
When such a discourse as this is being spoken, there arises doubt, there arises perplexity;

one who has not attained forms the notion that he has attained, one who has not mastered forms the notion that he has mastered, one who has not realized forms the notion that he has realized; being pained and dejected, he feels remorse and is frustrated, falling into despondency.
For what reason?
Because this matter is profound, namely, specific conditionality and dependent origination.
Furthermore, this state is even more difficult to see: the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and nirvāṇa.
NidSa 11.5: These two are the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Therein, of the conditioned, arising is discerned, passing away is discerned, and change-while-enduring is also discerned.
Of the unconditioned, neither arising is discerned, nor passing away, nor change-while-enduring.
"Thus, monks, conditioned phenomena are suffering;
Nirvana is peace.
From the arising of a cause comes the arising of suffering."
From the cessation of the cause comes the cessation of suffering;
the path is cut off and does not proceed;
it ceases without further rebirth.

"This indeed is the end of suffering. (NidSa 11.7) "In this regard, monks, who has attained final nirvana? It is none other than that which is the cessation of suffering, its subsiding, its becoming cooled, and its passing away.
Peaceful is this state, namely: the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and nirvana."
Sūtra 12: Obstructed (nivṛta) NidSa 12.1: For a fool who is obstructed by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body together with consciousness has thus arisen for that unlearned, ordinary person.
Thus, there is both this body of his together with consciousness and external name-and-form.
Thus there is a dyad.
Dependent upon a dyad, indeed, arises contact.
There are these six bases of contact, by which the unlearned, ordinary person—being touched again and again—experiences pleasure and pain.
Or again, taking this as a basis, or by means of any one of these:
What are the six?
The eye-sphere of contact (cakṣuḥ-sparśāyatana).
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are the bases of contact (*sparśāyatana*).
For a wise person who is obscured by ignorance and bound by craving, this body together with consciousness has thus arisen.
Thus, there is both this body of his together with consciousness and external name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Thus there are two. Dependent upon these two, indeed, is contact. There are these six bases of contact, by which a wise person, being touched again and again, experiences pleasure and pain.
Or again, based on this, or by means of any one of these:
what are the six?
The sphere of visual contact, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind.

NidSa 12.7: "Thus, monks, what is the distinction, what is the intention, what is the difference between a fool and a wise person regarding their dwelling in the holy life (brahmacarya) in my presence? NidSa 12.8: "Venerable Sir, all phenomena have the Blessed One as their root," and so on as before, up to: "I shall speak. NidSa 12.9: "By whatever ignorance (avidyā) the fool—the unlearned ordinary person—is shrouded, and by whatever craving (tṛṣṇā) he is bound, this body together with consciousness has come to be; and that [ignorance and craving]..."
Ignorance has not been abandoned and that craving has not been exhausted.
Because of the non-abandonment of that ignorance and the non-exhaustion of that craving, after the breaking up of the body, following death, he becomes one who goes to a body.
Being one who goes to a body, he is not fully liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.
"I say that he is not liberated from suffering.
Why is that?
Because in the past, the fool did not practice the holy life (brahmacarya) for the sake of the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering."
Therefore, after the breaking up of the body, following death, he becomes one who has gone to the body.

Being one who has gone to the body, he is not fully released from suffering, as before; so I say. Now, that ignorance by which the body together with consciousness was produced for the wise man who was obscured, and that craving to which he was bound—both that ignorance and that [craving] have been abandoned.
And craving is completely exhausted.
Through the abandonment of that ignorance and the total exhaustion of that craving, after the breaking up of the body and after death, he does not go to a [new] body.
Not going to a body, he is fully liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair.
"I say that he is completely liberated from suffering.
For what reason?
Because the wise one previously practiced the search for the holy life for the sake of the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering."
Therefore, upon the breakup of the body after death, he does not go to the body.
Not going to the body, he is fully liberated from suffering, as previously stated.
Monks, this is the distinction, this is the intention, this is the difference between the fool and the wise man regarding their dwelling in the holy life under me.
Sūtra 13: Not Yours 13.1 "Monks, this body is not yours, nor does it belong to others. These six spheres of contact were previously conditioned and intended."
I say that past karma is to be understood.
NidSa 13.2: Which six?
The sphere of visual contact.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are the bases of contact.
In this regard, the learned noble disciple thoroughly, correctly, and fundamentally contemplates dependent origination itself:
namely, that when this exists, the six groups of consciousness come to be.
There are six groups of contact, six groups of feeling, six groups of perception, and six groups of volition;
that is to say, when this exists, there arise in the future birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
NidSa 13.5: Thus, with cause and with condition, the world arises;
thus, there is the arising of the world with its cause and its condition.
NidSa 13.6: That is to say, when this is absent, the six groups of consciousness do not come to be.
The six groups of contact, the six groups of feeling, the six groups of perception, and the six groups of volition do not exist.
That is to say, when these are absent, in this way, in the future, birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair cease.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.

And when a learned noble disciple has, by means of right wisdom, correctly seen, thoroughly known, fully experienced, and deeply penetrated the origin of the world and the cessation of the world as they truly are, he is called a noble disciple. He is said to have come to this true Dharma, approached this true Dharma, and understood the true Dharma; he is one who has reached deep penetration.

Having fully penetrated and attained [this state] through the knowledge of a trainee and the vision of a trainee, he is endowed with the noble, world-transcending wisdom that rises and sets with the world— a wisdom that leads to liberation and penetration— and thus he goes forth, performing that which effects the complete destruction of suffering and the final end of suffering.
For what reason?
Because the learned noble disciple has, by means of right wisdom, seen, known, and thoroughly penetrated the origin of the world and the cessation of the world as they truly are.

Sūtra 14: (Dependent Origination) NidSa 14.1: "Monks, I shall teach you dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and dependently originated phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharmāḥ*). Listen to them, and attend to them well and thoroughly; I shall speak."
NidSa 14.2: What is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)? It is this: when this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises.
That is to say: with ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and so on, until there is the arising [of the whole mass of suffering].

“Conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces (saṃskāra). Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the realm for the stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā-dhātu), remains fixed. Having personally realized and fully awakened to this, the Tathāgata declares it, makes it known, establishes it, analyzes it, discloses it, clarifies it, teaches it, and reveals it—namely, that conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces.”

NidSa 14.4–5: "With birth as condition, there is aging and death"—whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the realm for the stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā-dhātu), remains fixed. Having personally realized and fully awakened to this, the Tathāgata declares it, makes it known, establishes it, analyzes it, discloses it, clarifies it, teaches it, and reveals it; namely: [the rest of the dependent origination formula].
"Old age and death have birth as their condition.

(NidSa 14.6) This which is here the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), the fixed course of phenomena (*dharma-niyāmatā*), the suchness of phenomena (*dharma-yathātathā*),
non-falsity, non-alteration, reality, truth, actuality, suchness, non-perversion, non-inversion, and specific conditionality (*idaṃpratyayatā*).
Conformity with dependent origination—
this is called dependent origination.
What are dependently originated phenomena?

Ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age and death—these are called dependently arisen phenomena.
And when a learned noble disciple has clearly seen with right wisdom, as it truly is, both dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena, [he is liberated]. (NidSa 14.8)
He does not look back to the past,
thinking: "Did I indeed exist in the past,
or did I not exist in the past?"
"Who indeed was I in the past?
How indeed was I in the past? Thus one does not look back toward the prior limit. *Nidānasamyukta* 14.10.
"Shall I exist in the future?
Or shall I not exist in the future? What shall I become in the future?"
"How indeed shall I be in the future time?"—thus one becomes inwardly full of doubt and uncertainty: "What indeed is this? *NidSa* 14.11.
What indeed is this? Who being what, what shall we become? From where has this sentient being come?
Having passed away from here, where will he go?

NidSa 14.12: Whatever various speculative views there are among certain recluses and brahmins in the world—namely, those associated with the doctrine of a self, those associated with the doctrine of a sentient being, those associated with the doctrine of a soul, and those associated with the doctrine of wonders and auspicious omens.

At that time, those [defilements] of his have been abandoned, fully understood, cut off at the root like the stump of a palm tree, rendered incapable of further existence, and subject to the law of non-arising in the future.
Why is that? NidSa 14.13. Because:

For it is thus: by the learned noble disciple, dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena have been well seen, well attended to, well understood, and well penetrated with right wisdom as they truly are.
Sūtra 15: Emptiness (śūnyatā).
NidSa 15.1: The setting was among the Kurus.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

"I shall teach you the Dharma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end—which I shall reveal in its entirety. Listen to this discourse on the Dharma called 'The Great Emptiness' (Mahāśūnyatā); attend to it well and thoroughly, and I shall speak."
NidSa 15.4: What are the discourses on the great emptiness?
Namely: "When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.
That is to say: conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces, and so on, until there is the arising [of the whole mass of suffering].
"Old age and death have birth as their condition.
In this regard, there might be questioners who ask, "What is old age and death? Or to whom does old age and death belong?
To such people, one should say: "This is old age and death; or this is the old age and death of that [person]."
And if someone were to say: "That which is the soul is the body," or "The soul is one thing and the body is another," both of these are one;
only the expression here is different.
“Monks, when the view ‘the soul is the same as the body’ exists, the living of the holy life does not occur;
when the view ‘the soul is one thing and the body another’ exists, the living of the holy life does not occur.
Without approaching either of these two extremes, there is the middle way—a noble, supramundane, true, non-perverted right view.”
That is to say: conditioned by birth, there is aging and death;
likewise, birth, becoming, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, and consciousness [are each conditioned by their respective antecedents].
Thus: conditioned by ignorance, there are volitional formations.
In that regard, there might be questioners who ask, "What are the formations? or "Whose are the formations?

To whomsoever one might say, "These are the formations," or "These are the formations of this [person]," and to whomsoever one might say, "The soul is the same as the body" or "The soul is one thing and the body another."
Both of these are one; only the phrasing here is different. "Monks, when the view that 'the soul is the same as the body' exists, the life of celibacy does not come to be. (NidSa 15.7b)
When there is the view that the soul is one thing and the body another, the life of celibacy does not come to pass.
Not approaching these two extremes, there is the middle way—noble, supramundane, in accordance with reality, non-perverted, and right view—which is as follows:
namely, "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces."
And when, for a monk, ignorance has faded away and true knowledge has arisen:
(8b) for him, who is there that has old age and death, or whose is old age and death?

(8c) Through the fading away of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge, his old age and death are thus abandoned, fully understood, cut off at the root like the top of a palm tree, rendered incapable of further becoming in the future.
The nature of non-arising.
NidSa 15.9a: And when, for a monk, ignorance has faded away and knowledge has arisen, NidSa 15.9b:
for him there is no birth, becoming, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, or consciousness.
NidSa 15.10b: What are his volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), or to whom do these volitional formations belong?

NidSa 15.10c: Through the fading away of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge, in this way those volitional formations of his are abandoned and fully understood; they are cut off at the root like the top of a palm tree, deprived of the condition for future existence, and subject to the law of non-arising in the future.
And when, for a monk, ignorance has faded away and knowledge has arisen—
NidSa 15.11b through the cessation of that ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations, up to the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
NidSa 15.12 This is called the Dharma discourse named "The Great Emptiness."
"I will teach you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and [good] in the end," as I have said before—this is what was meant by that statement.
Sūtra 16: The Opening Discourse (NidSa 16.1) "Monks, I shall teach you the beginning of dependent origination and its analysis. Listen to it; attend to it well and thoroughly, and I shall speak."
NidSa 16.2: What is the beginning of dependent origination? It is this: when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. That is to say:
conditioned by ignorance are the volitional formations, and so on as before, until there is the arising of the whole mass of suffering.
This is called the beginning of dependent origination.
What is the analysis?
"Conditioned by ignorance are the formations"—what is ignorance?

That which is ignorance regarding the past, ignorance regarding the future, ignorance regarding both the past and the future; ignorance regarding the internal, ignorance regarding the external, ignorance regarding both the internal and the external; ignorance regarding action, ignorance regarding its maturation; ignorance regarding the Buddha, ignorance regarding the Dharma, ignorance regarding the Saṅgha;
ignorance regarding suffering, ignorance regarding its origin, ignorance regarding its cessation, and ignorance regarding the path; and ignorance regarding causality.

Ignorance is ignorance regarding phenomena arisen from causes; it is ignorance regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome, what is blameworthy and blameless, what is to be cultivated and not to be cultivated, what is inferior and superior, what is dark and bright, and ignorance regarding phenomena that have arisen dependently in their respective parts.
Furthermore, it is the lack of penetration into the six bases of contact as they truly are.

Wherever there is ignorance, non-seeing, lack of clear realization, darkness, delusion, and the latent tendency of ignorance—this is called ignorance. (NidSa 16.5) "With ignorance as a condition, there are volitional formations. What are volitional formations?
There are three formative forces (*saṃskāra*):
the formative force of body, the formative force of speech, and the formative force of mind.
Regarding the statement "consciousness has formative forces as its condition," what is consciousness?
The six groups of consciousness:
eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
Regarding the statement, "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form [arises]," what is name-and-form?
There are four formless aggregates:
the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
What is the aggregate of form?
Whatever form there may be, all that consists of the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements; this is form,
and the aforementioned is name.
Both of those together are called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
Regarding the statement, "With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise": what are the six sense bases?
There are six internal sense bases (*āyatana*).
The eye is an internal sense base; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are internal sense bases.
(NidSa 16.9) "With the six sense bases as condition, there is contact (*sparśa*). What is contact?
The six groups of contact: visual contact,
and auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental contact.
"Feeling has contact as its condition. What is feeling?
There are three feelings:
pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
"Conditioned by feeling is craving. What is craving?
There are three types of craving:
craving for sensual pleasures, craving for form, and craving for the formless.
NidSa 16.12: "With craving as condition, there is grasping. What is grasping? There are four kinds of grasping:
grasping at sensual pleasures, grasping at views, grasping at rules and observances, and grasping at a self.
"Existence has grasping as its condition. What is existence?
There are three existences:
existence in the realm of desire, existence in the realm of form, and existence in the formless realm.
“With existence as condition, birth” — what is birth? It is the birth,

the being born, the descent, the manifestation, the appearance, the acquisition of the aggregates, the acquisition of the elements, the acquisition of the sense bases, and the manifestation of the life-faculty of those various sentient beings within their respective classes of beings.
This is called birth.
Regarding the statement "conditioned by birth is aging-and-death," what is aging?
It is that which consists of baldness, graying hair, abundance of wrinkles, decrepitude, brokenness, the curvature of the back like a roof-rafter, and a body that breathes with a wheezing sound.
The state of having a body bent forward, leaning on a staff, with limbs marked by moles and wrinkles; slowness, decline, and deterioration;
the maturation and disintegration of the sense faculties; the state of being worn out and decrepit of the conditioned formations—this is called aging.
What is death? It is the passing away,

the falling away, the breaking up, the disappearance, the loss of life, the loss of heat, the cessation of vitality, the casting off of the aggregates, death, and the completion of one's time for those various beings from their respective classes of beings.
This is called death; thus,
this is death and the aforementioned aging.
Both of these together are called "aging and death.
This is called the analysis of dependent origination.
As for what was said by me: "I shall teach you the beginning of dependent origination and its analysis," this is that which has been explained.
Sūtra 17: The Monk.
NidSa 17.1: A certain monk approached the Blessed One;
having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, that monk said this to the Blessed One:
"NidSa 17.2 Was dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) created by the Blessed One, or rather by others? NidSa 17.3 It was not created by me, O monk, nor was it created by others."
Moreover, whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this very nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the element for the stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā-dhātu), remains fixed.
Having personally realized and fully awakened to it, the Tathāgata declares it, makes it known, establishes it, analyzes it, reveals it, makes it plain, teaches it, and elucidates it—namely:
"When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises."
