That is to say: conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces, up to their arising and their cessation.
Sūtra 18: A certain brahmin approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, that brahmin said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Gautama, does he who acts experience [the result]?
"Brahmin, I have left this undeclared: that he who acts experiences [the result]."
NidSa 18.3: "Venerable Gautama, does one person act and another experience [the result]?
"Brahmin, that too has been left undeclared by me: that one person acts and another experiences [the result].
NidSa 18.4: "Venerable Gautama, when asked, 'Does the very same person who acts also experience [the result]?', you say it is undeclared."
"When asked whether one person acts and another experiences [the result], you say it is undeclared.
But what, Master Gautama, is the meaning of this statement to be understood? "O Brahmin, to say 'he who acts is he who experiences' leads to the view of eternalism."
"One person acts and another experiences [the result]"—this leads to the extreme of annihilationism.
Without resorting to these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma by way of the middle way:
namely, "when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises."
That is to say: "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces," up to the arising and the cessation [of suffering].
Sūtra 19: Kātyāyana.
NidSa 19.1: The Blessed One was staying at Nādika in the Guñjikāvasatha.
Then the venerable Sandhākātyāyana approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the venerable Sandhākātyāyana addressed the Blessed One in this way:
NidSa 19.3: "Venerable sir, it is said: 'right view, right view.
To what extent is there right view?
To what extent does the Tathāgata, when designating right view, designate it?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Sandhākātyāyana:

"Kātyāyana, this world relies on a duality; for the most part, it relies on existence and non-existence. Kātyāyana, this world is bound by attachment and clinging; that is to say, it relies on existence and non-existence."

If one does not approach, does not grasp, does not dwell upon, and does not adhere to these bases of attachment— the acquisitions of the mind— as being "this is my self," then this suffering, when arising, arises; and this suffering,
when ceasing, ceases.
If, in this regard, one does not hesitate and does not doubt,
his knowledge becomes independent of others. To this extent, Kātyāyana, right view comes to be.
To this extent, the Tathāgata, when designating right view, designates it.
Why is that? Kātyāyana, for one who sees the origin of the world as it really is with correct wisdom, that non-existence which belongs to the world does not occur.
For one who sees the cessation of the world as it truly is with right wisdom, that which constitutes existence in the world does not come to be.
(NidSa 19.8) Not approaching these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma by means of the middle way.
(NidSa 19.9) That is to say: when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.
Namely: "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise," and so on as before, up to their origin and their cessation.
While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the mind of the Venerable Sandhākātyāyana was liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.
Sūtra 20: The Naked Ascetic (Acela)

NidSa 20.1 The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain. NidSa 20.2 Then, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One descended from Vulture Peak Mountain and entered Rājagṛha for alms.
NidSa 20.3 Now at that time, the naked ascetic Kāśyapa had set out for alms in Rājagṛha for some particular business.
Acelaka Kāśyapa saw the Blessed One from afar;
having seen him, he approached the Blessed One,
and upon reaching him, he said this to the Blessed One:

NidSa 20.4: "Venerable Gautama, we would ask you about a certain matter, if you would grant us the opportunity to have our question answered. NidSa 20.5: "It is not yet the right time for you, Kāśyapa, to have your question answered."
First, you must wander for alms in Rājagṛha; go outside the monastery,
and there the time will come for you to answer the question.
NidSa 20.6 This should be repeated a second time in the same way.
NidSa 20.7 A third time, Acelaka Āśyapa said this to the Blessed One:
"It might be, Master Gautama, that there would be an obstacle for us, were Gautama to change his mind."
"Right here we ask you, venerable Gautama; if you would grant us the opportunity to answer our question. "Ask, Kāśyapa, whatever you desire."
"Master Gautama, is suffering self-made?
"Kāśyapa, this has not been declared by me: that suffering is self-made. "Master Gautama, is suffering made by another?"
"Kāśyapa, this too has been left undeclared by me: that suffering is created by another.
‘Venerable Gautama, is suffering both self-created and created by another?
Kāśyapa, this too has been left undeclared by me: that suffering is both self-created and created by another."
“Venerable Gautama, is suffering then produced neither by oneself nor by another, but arisen without cause?
“Kāśyapa, that too has been left undeclared by me: that suffering is produced neither by oneself nor by another, but arisen without cause.
“Venerable Gautama, when asked, ‘Is suffering created by oneself? you say it is undeclared.”

When asked whether suffering is caused by another, caused by oneself, caused by both another and oneself, or whether it arises without being caused by self-action or action by another, you say it is undeclared.
"But Master Gautama, does suffering not exist at all?
"Kāśyapa, it is not that suffering does not exist; rather, suffering certainly exists."
"Venerable Gautama, please teach me the Dharma in such a way that I may know suffering and see suffering.
"Kāśyapa, if one were to think, 'That very feeling is the one who feels,' and thus maintain that suffering is self-made,
I do not say that."
NidSa 20.13b: "The feeling is one thing, and the feeler is another"—if one should think thus, that suffering is created by another, I do not say this.
NidSa 20.13c: "For one who exists as being overwhelmed by feeling, others heap up suffering"—if one should think thus, that suffering is both self-created and created by another.

Even so, I do not say that there are sufferings due to ten conditions. If one were to think thus: "Suffering is produced neither by oneself nor by another, but arises without a cause," it is this [view] that I do not say.
NidSa 20.14: Not approaching these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma by means of the middle way:
namely, "When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises," and so on, as before, up to the arising and the cessation [of suffering].
NidSa 20.15: While this discourse on the Dharma was being spoken, the dust-free, stainless eye of Dharma regarding all phenomena arose in Acelaka Kāśyapa.
Then Acelaka Kāśyapa, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, and plunged deeply into the Dharma—

having crossed beyond doubt, crossed beyond perplexity, being independent of others and no longer led by others, having attained fearlessness regarding the teachings in the Teacher’s instruction— bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"I have gone for refuge, Blessed One; I have gone for refuge! I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks.
May you accept me as a lay follower from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, one who has gone for refuge and is full of faith."
NidSa 20.18 Then Acelaka Kāśyapa, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet and departed from the Blessed One’s presence.
NidSa 20.19 Not long after Acelaka Kāśyapa had departed from the Blessed One’s presence, he was deprived of life by a cow with a young calf.
At the time of his death, his faculties were serene, the color of his face was pure, and the color of his skin was radiant.
NidSa 20.20 Then, a large number of monks, having dressed in the forenoon and taken their bowls and robes, entered Rājagṛha for alms.
While wandering for alms in Rājagṛha, those many monks heard:

"That Acelaka Kāśyapa, who had questioned the Blessed One regarding a matter in Rājagṛha, has not long since departed from the presence of the Blessed One when he was deprived of life by a cow with a young calf."
At the time of his death, his faculties were serene, the color of his face was pure, and the complexion of his skin was bright.

Having heard this, they then went for alms in Rājagṛha; having finished their meal and returned from their alms-round after the meal, they put away their bowls and robes, washed their feet, and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the many monks said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, here we, many monks, having dressed in the morning and taken our bowls and robes, entered Rājagṛha for alms."
"We, a great many monks, heard while wandering for alms in Rājagṛha—as previously described—up until: 'his complexion was perfectly clear.
Venerable sir, what is his destination? What is his rebirth? What is his future state?
"Monks, that son of good family belongs to the class of those who possess material substance."

"And that noble son recognized the secondary dharma within my teachings; he did not contradict the discourse I had delivered concerning the matters of the Dharma. Perform the worship of his body with his remains."
Thereupon, the Blessed One gave the supreme prediction concerning Acelaka Kāśyapa.
Sūtra 21: Timburuka, NidSa 21.1. This very same sūtra [is] the *Timburuka-parivrājaka*.
NidSa 21.2. The distinction is that he asks about pleasure and pain.
Sūtra 22: The Chapter on the Grounds (Bhūmika) NidSa 22.1:
The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
NidSa 22.2: At that time, the Venerable Bhūmika was staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain.

NidSa 22.3 Then a great number of wandering mendicants of other sects approached the Venerable Bhūmika. Having approached, they exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the Venerable Bhūmika and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the great number of wandering mendicants of other sects said this to the Venerable Bhūmika:
NidSa 22.4: "Venerable Bhūmika, let us ask you about a certain point, if you would grant the opportunity for an answer to our question. NidSa 22.5: "Ask, sirs."
"Having heard it, I shall inform you.
"Venerable Bhūmika, is pleasure and pain self-made?
"This has been left undeclared by the Blessed One, Venerable Sir: that pleasure and pain are self-made."
NidSa 22.6b: “Master Bhūmika, is pleasure and pain created by another, created by both self and another, or produced without being created by self or another?

“Venerable sir, this too has been left undeclared by the Blessed One: whether pleasure and pain are created by another, created by both self and another, or produced without being created by self or another.
NidSa 22.7: “Master Bhūmika, when asked, ‘Is pleasure and pain created by oneself? you say it is undeclared.”

When asked whether pleasure and pain are caused by another, caused by oneself, caused by both another and oneself, or produced without being caused by either oneself or another, you declared them to be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
How, then, has pleasure and pain been described as having arisen by the Blessed One Gautama?
"Sirs, pleasure and pain have been described by the Blessed One as dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*)."

NidSa 22.9 Then many wandering mendicants of other sects neither approved nor rejected what the venerable Bhūmika had said; and having neither approved nor rejected it, they rose from their seats and departed.
NidSa 22.10 Now at that time, the venerable Śāriputra was sitting not far from the venerable Bhūmika, leaning against the foot of a certain tree.
Then the Venerable Bhūmika, having perceived that many wanderers of other sects had recently departed, approached the Venerable Śāriputra.
Having approached him, he reported in detail to the Venerable Śāriputra everything that had been the subject of their conversation with those many wanderers of other sects,
and spoke as follows:
"Venerable Śāriputra, by answering in this way, am I not misrepresenting the Blessed One?
Do I not overstep him?
Do I speak what was said by the Blessed One, and do I speak in accordance with the Dharma?"
I declare the Dharma and its subsequent practice,

and no one shall come from another to engage me in a formal debate or counter-argument on the basis of the Dharma with a point that deserves censure. Therefore, Venerable Bhūmika, by answering truthfully, you do not misrepresent the Blessed One.
You do not overstep [the truth];
you speak what has been said by the Blessed One and speak according to the Dharma;
and you explain the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
And no one else shall come from outside to challenge you with a reasoned argument regarding this point of reproach.
Why is that?
Because, venerable Bhūmika, the Blessed One has designated pleasure and pain as dependently originated.
In this regard, venerable sir, as for those ascetics and brahmins who designate pleasure and pain as self-made, that too is dependently arisen.
That it would be something not dependently arisen—
such a case is impossible.

They designate pleasure and pain as being caused by another, caused by oneself, caused by both another and oneself, or as arising without being caused by oneself or another; yet even that is dependently originated.
Indeed, that which is dependently originated will indeed be dependently originated.
This is impossible.
In this regard, venerable sir, as for those ascetics and brahmins who designate pleasure and pain as self-made, that too has contact as its condition.
How could they, indeed, experience it apart from contact?
This is impossible:

that they should designate pleasure and pain as being both caused by another and caused by oneself, or as caused by both another and oneself, or as arising without being caused by oneself or another— that too has contact as its condition.
"Indeed, it is impossible that they would experience [the result] apart from contact;
such a case does not exist.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was sitting not far from the Venerable Śāriputra, leaning against the foot of a certain tree.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having grasped and mastered everything that had been the conversation between the Venerable Bhūmika and the Venerable Śāriputra,
approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
While standing to one side, the Venerable Ānanda reported in detail to the Blessed One everything that had been the subject of conversation between the Venerable Bhūmika and the Venerable Śāriputra.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Excellent, excellent, Ānanda! The monk Śāriputra is wise."

When the deceased asked a question and it was answered by one possessed of right wisdom, I desire that some disciple, when questioned by the deceased, might answer just as it was answered by the monk Śāriputra. At one time: [NidSa 22.20] At one time, on a certain occasion: [NidSa 22.20]
I dwell at Rājagṛha in the Girivraja.

There, certain wanderers of other sects asked me this very same matter in these words and with these syllables. To them, when questioned, I explained this very matter in these words and with these syllables, just as it was done by the monk Śāriputra.
In this regard, whatever ascetics or brahmins there may be who designate pleasure and pain as self-made, I approach them;
having approached, I say this:
"Is it true, sirs, that you designate pleasure and pain as self-made?"
When I questioned them, they affirmed, "It is so. To them I said,
"Venerable sirs, it is indeed as you have stated."
Furthermore, regarding that which you, sirs, grasp with force, adhere to, and continue to assert—
claiming "this alone is the truth, all else is delusion"—
I do not grant permission for this here.
For what reason?
Because, sirs, I have designated pleasure and pain as having arisen from other causes;
yet they question me about this.
"How has pleasure and pain been designated by the Blessed One Gautama as arisen?
To them I say:
"Pleasure and pain have been designated by me as dependently arisen."

NidSa 22.23: “Those who designate pleasure and pain as being caused by another, or caused by oneself, or caused by both another and oneself, or as arising without being caused by oneself or another—I shall approach them... [as before] ...up to:
NidSa 22.24: “Indeed, venerable sir, as I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has said, when there is birth, aging and death come to be.”
There is no aging and death other than with birth as their condition;
likewise, as long as ignorance exists, the formative forces come to be,
and there are no formative forces other than with ignorance as their condition.
NidSa 22.25 Thus should cessation be described. NidSa 22.26 The Blessed One restates this very point to the venerable Ānanda.
Sūtra 23: One endowed with right view.
The setting was Rājagṛha. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila were staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila rose from his seclusion and went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was.
Having approached and exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the Venerable Śāriputra face-to-face, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila said this to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, let us ask about a certain matter."
"If you would grant me the opportunity to answer this question,
venerable Mahākauṣṭhila,
ask; having heard it, I shall explain it to you."
"To what extent, venerable Śāriputra, is a noble disciple in this Dharma and Vinaya one who is endowed with right view, who is possessed of an upright view,
and who is endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha?"
"Having come to this True Dharma, having approached this True Dharma, one understands the True Dharma"—thus it is said.
Mahākoṣṭhila, because this noble disciple understands what is unwholesome as it truly is, and understands the root of the unwholesome as it truly is... [NidSa 23.7a]"
He understands the wholesome as it really is;
he understands the root of the wholesome as it really is. What is the unwholesome? He understands it as it really is.
Unwholesome bodily action, verbal action, and mental action—
this is unwholesome.
In this way, one understands the unwholesome as it truly is.

What does one understand as it really is regarding the unwholesome roots? There are three unwholesome roots: greed is an unwholesome root; [hatred is an unwholesome root; delusion is an unwholesome root].
Hatred and delusion are unwholesome roots;
this is an unwholesome root.
In this way, one understands the unwholesome roots as they truly are.
Wholesome bodily action, vocal action, and mental action— this is wholesome.
In this way, one understands wholesomeness as it truly is.

What are the wholesome roots that one understands as they really are? There are three wholesome roots: non-greed is a wholesome root; [non-hatred is a wholesome root; non-delusion is a wholesome root].
Non-hatred and non-delusion are wholesome roots;
this is a wholesome root.
In this way, one understands the wholesome root as it truly is.
And because, venerable Mahākoṣṭhila, a noble disciple thus understands the unwholesome as it really is,
understands the root of the unwholesome as it really is,
and understands the wholesome as it really is.
He understands the roots of wholesome merit as they truly are.
To this extent, a noble disciple in this Dharma and Vinaya becomes one perfected in view,
and he becomes endowed with a straightforward view.
He becomes endowed with verified clarity regarding the Buddha;
having come to this True Dharma and approached this True Dharma, he understands the True Dharma—thus he is called one who has understood the True Dharma.
[NidSa 23.8] "Venerable Śāriputra, is this the only way?"
"Could it be someone else?
"It could be someone else, Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila.
"Insofar as a noble disciple understands the nutriments as they truly are..."
He understands, as it truly is, the origin of nutriment, the cessation of nutriment, and the practice leading to the cessation of nutriment.
What does he understand, as it truly is, regarding nutriments?
There are four nutriments.
Edible food is twofold: gross and subtle.
Contact is the second.
Mental volition is the third.
Consciousness is the fourth.
These are the nutriments.
Thus he understands the nutriments as they truly are.
What is the arising of nutriment as it really is?
Craving, which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there;
this is the arising of nutriment.

In this way, one understands the origin of nutriment as it really is. What is the cessation of nutriment as it really is? It is the complete abandoning, relinquishing, casting off, destruction, fading away, and cessation of that very craving which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust, and finds delight here and there.
Cessation, tranquility, and disappearance—
this is the cessation of nutriment.
In this way, one understands the cessation of nutriment as it truly is.
What is the practice leading to the cessation of nutriment that he understands as it really is?
That is to say, the noble eightfold path:
namely, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
This is the path;
this is the practice leading to the cessation of nutriment.
In this way, he understands, as it truly is, the practice leading to the cessation of nutriment.
And because the noble disciple thus understands these nutriments as they really are—
understands the arising of nutriment, the cessation of nutriment, and the practice leading to the cessation of nutriment as they really are—
to this extent, the noble disciple is one who has attained right view in this Dharma and Vinaya, as previously described.
“Venerable Śāriputra, is this the only way of explaining it,
or is there another?
“Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, there may be another.”
NidSa 23.11a When a noble disciple understands the outflows as they really are,
he understands the origin of the outflows, the cessation of the outflows, and the path leading to the cessation of the outflows as they really are.
NidSa 23.11b What are the outflows that he understands as they really are?
There are three outflows:
the outflow of sensual desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance.
These are the outflows.
In this way, one understands the outflows as they really are.
What is the arising of the outflows as it really is? From the arising of ignorance comes the arising of the outflows.
This is the origin of the taints.
In this way, one understands the origin of the taints as it truly is.
What is the cessation of the taints that one understands as it truly is?
From the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of the outflows;
thus one understands the cessation of the outflows as it truly is. What is the path leading to the cessation of the outflows that one understands as it truly is?
The noble eightfold path is as previously described.
And because the noble disciple thus understands the outflows as they really are,
he understands the origin of the outflows, the cessation of the outflows, and the practice leading to the cessation of the outflows as they really are.
"In this much, a noble disciple becomes one who is perfected in view within this Dharma and Vinaya, as before.
"Venerable Śāriputra, is this the only way of explaining it,
or is there another?"
"It may be so, venerable Mahākoṣṭhila.
Furthermore, it is because the noble disciple understands suffering as it really is;
he understands the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice leading to the cessation of suffering as they really are."
What does one understand as it really is regarding suffering? Birth is suffering;
aging is suffering.
Sickness is suffering;
death is suffering;
separation from the beloved is suffering.
Association with the unpleasant is suffering;
not obtaining what one desires and seeks after is also suffering;
in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
"This is suffering.
In this way, one understands suffering as it truly is. What is the origin of suffering? One understands the origin of suffering as it truly is.
Craving leading to renewed existence is as previously described;
this is the origin of suffering.
In this way, one understands the origin of suffering as it truly is.
What is the cessation of suffering as it really is?
It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving which leads to renewed existence, as described before;
this is the cessation of suffering.
In this way, one understands the cessation of suffering as it really is.
What is the path leading to the cessation of suffering that one understands as it really is?
It is the noble eightfold path, as described previously.
This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, one understands the practice leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is.
NidSa 23.13f.
"To this extent, a noble disciple becomes one who is perfected in view within this Dharma and Vinaya, as previously stated.
"Venerable Śāriputra, is this the only way of explaining it,
or is there another?"
"Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila, there may be another [reason] as well:
because a noble disciple understands aging and death as they truly are;
he understands the origin of aging and death, the cessation of aging and death, and the practice leading to the cessation of aging and death as they truly are."
NidSa 23.15b: What is it that understands aging and death as they really are?
As before, as in the introductory sūtra.
NidSa 23.15c: What is it that understands the origin of aging and death as it really is?
From the arising of birth comes the arising of aging and death.
Thus, from the cessation of birth comes the cessation of aging and death.
The noble eightfold path is as previously described.
And when a noble disciple thus understands aging and death as they really are,
understands the origin of aging and death, the cessation of aging and death, and the practice leading to the cessation of aging and death as they really are—
to this extent, a noble disciple becomes one who has perfected vision in this Dharma and Vinaya, as described previously.
In this way, birth, becoming, clinging, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and volitional formations [are to be understood].

(NidSa 23.16) And because the noble disciple understands volitional formations as they really are, he understands the arising of volitional formations, the cessation of volitional formations, and the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations as they really are. (NidSa 23.17a)
What is it that one understands as they really are regarding the formative forces?
There are three formative forces:
the bodily formation, the vocal formation, and the mental formation.
NidSa 23.17c: What is the arising of volitional formations as it really is? From the arising of ignorance comes the arising of volitional formations;
this is the arising of volitional formations.
In this way, one understands the arising of volitional formations as it really is. What is the cessation of volitional formations as it really is?
With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations.

This is the cessation of volitional formations. What is the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations? He understands it as it really is: the noble eightfold path, as described before.
"Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila, when a noble disciple thus understands the conditioned phenomena as they really are—
understands the origin of conditioned phenomena, the cessation of conditioned phenomena, and the path leading to the cessation of conditioned phenomena as they really are—
to this extent, a noble disciple is one who has perfected the view in this Dharma and Vinaya."
He is endowed with upright vision and is endowed with verified clarity regarding the Buddha.
Having come to this True Dharma and approached this True Dharma, he understands the True Dharma; thus he is called one who "understands the True Dharma."
“Venerable Śāriputra, is this the only way of explaining it,
or is there another as well?
“You are overreaching, you are overreaching, venerable Mahākauṣṭhila!”
"You will not be able to grasp the questions to their ultimate limit, because for a disciple in training, ignorance has been detached from and knowledge has arisen.
"Then what further remains to be done? Having thus rejoiced and approved of each other's words, those two good men rose from their seats and departed.
Sūtra 24: This is the reality. Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāriputra:
"Śāriputra, this was said by me in the *Parāyaṇa* among the 'Questions of Ajita'."
And those who have mastered the Dharma, and those various types of trainees— for them all, observe my diligent conduct.
Being asked, speak, O worthy one!
“Śāriputra, who are those in training (śaikṣa), and what are the dharmas that have been fully analyzed?
When this was said, the Venerable Śāriputra remained silent.
A second and even a third time, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Venerable Śāriputra.
“Śāriputra, this was said by me in the *Parāyaṇa* among the *Ajita* questions: ‘And those who have analyzed the Dharma,’ as before. A second and a third time, the Venerable Śāriputra remained silent.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāriputra:
"Śāriputra, this is real.
"It is so, Venerable Sir; this is real."
"Venerable sir, when a monk is practicing for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what has come to be, he is then practicing for disenchantment, dispassion,
and cessation regarding that which arises from nutriment.
When he is practicing for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding that which arises from nutriment, [he is practicing for the cessation of suffering]."
“Regarding ‘the cessation of that nutriment’:
having understood that whatever has come to be is subject to cessation, a monk practices for the sake of disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation with respect to what is subject to cessation.
These are called those in training (śaikṣas).”
"Śāriputra, this is real. "So it is, Blessed One; this is real.

Through disenchantment with what is real, through dispassion toward it, and through its cessation, a monk becomes one whose mind is rightly and completely liberated from the outflows by way of non-clinging."
"Arising from that nutriment":

with regard to this arising from nutriment, a monk becomes one whose mind is rightly and completely liberated through disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, and non-clinging toward the outflows. "The cessation of that nutriment."

Having understood that whatever has come to be is subject to cessation, a monk—through weariness with what is subject to cessation, through dispassion toward it, and through its cessation—becomes rightly and completely liberated in mind by way of non-clinging regarding the outflows. These are called those who have fully comprehended the Dharma. Thus, Śāriputra, this is the reality.
"It is so, Śāriputra; for the sake of disenchantment and dispassion toward what has come to be," as before, up to "those who have reckoned the dharmas.
Then the Blessed One, having risen from his seat, entered his dwelling for seclusion.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra, knowing that the Blessed One had departed not long ago, addressed the monks:
"Venerable sirs, the Blessed One asked me this first question without my having anticipated it,
and I experienced an unprecedented state of confusion.
But when the Blessed One approved that first answer of mine, this thought occurred to me:"

"Venerable sir, if the Blessed One were to question me on this very same matter with different words and different phrases for an entire night, I, being questioned by the Blessed One on this very same matter with different words and different phrases, would be able to provide an answer for an entire night as well."
“Even if the Blessed One were to question me on this very same matter for one day, or one night and day, or even for seven nights and days, using different words and different phrases.”
"For seven days and nights, I could have answered this very same question for the Blessed One, having been asked it, using other words and other expressions.
(NidSa 24.25) Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One;
having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, that bhikṣu said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, the venerable Śāriputra has spoken noble words worthy of a seer; he has grasped [the matter] with certainty and let out a true lion’s roar in the assembly.
Venerable sirs, the Blessed One has addressed me regarding this as before."

"Venerable ones, if I were to question the Venerable Śāriputra on this very same matter using other words and other phrases for even an entire night, or even for seven days and nights, Śāriputra would provide the answer to this very matter when questioned with other words and other phrases."
NidSa 24.29: For in this way, the dharma-element has been thoroughly penetrated by the monk Śāriputra.
Sūtra 25: [The Discourse on] Inability.
NidSa 25.1: The setting was in Magadha.
"Monks, these three things exist that are undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable to the world.
Which three?
Namely: sickness, old age, and death."

If these three things— sickness, old age, and death— were not undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable to the world, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones would not appear in the world for the sake of proclaiming the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
But because sickness, old age, and death are these three things that are undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable, [Tathāgatas appear].
Therefore, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones arise in the world for the purpose of proclaiming the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
Without having abandoned three things, one is incapable of abandoning sickness, old age, and death. *Nidānasamyukta* 25.4.
Which three?
Namely, passion, hatred, and delusion.
Without abandoning these three factors, one is incapable of abandoning sickness, old age, and death.
NidSa 25.5: Without having abandoned three things, one is incapable of abandoning lust, hatred, and delusion.
Which three?
Namely: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the misapprehension of rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Without abandoning these three qualities, one is incapable of abandoning lust, hatred, and delusion.
Without abandoning three qualities, one is incapable of abandoning the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Which three?
Without abandoning these three factors— unwise attention, following wrong paths, and mental despondency—

one is incapable of abandoning the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*). Without abandoning these three factors, one is incapable of abandoning unwise attention, following wrong paths, and mental despondency.
Which three?
Forgetting mindfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and distraction.
Without abandoning these three factors, one is incapable of abandoning improper mental attention, the pursuit of wrong paths, and a sunken mind.
NidSa 25.8: Without abandoning three things, one is incapable of abandoning forgetfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and distraction.
Which three? Excitement, lack of restraint, and immoral conduct.
Without having abandoned these three qualities, one is incapable of abandoning forgetfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and distraction.
Without having abandoned three qualities, one is incapable of abandoning restlessness, lack of restraint, and immoral conduct.
Which three?
Without abandoning these three qualities— lack of faith, stinginess, and laziness— one is incapable of abandoning restlessness, lack of restraint, and immoral conduct.
Without abandoning three qualities, one is incapable of abandoning lack of faith, stinginess, and laziness.
Which three?

The desire not to see the noble ones, the desire not to hear the noble Dharma, and a mind intent on finding fault. Without abandoning these three qualities, one is incapable of abandoning lack of faith, stinginess, and laziness.
Without having abandoned three things, one is incapable of abandoning the lack of desire to see the noble ones, the lack of desire to hear the noble Dharma, and a mind intent on fault-finding.
Which three?
Disrespect, difficult speech, and association with evil friends.

Without having abandoned these three qualities, one is incapable of abandoning the lack of desire to see the noble ones, the lack of desire to hear the noble Dharma, and a mind intent on finding fault.
NidSa 25.12 Without having abandoned three qualities, one is incapable of abandoning disrespect, contumacy, and association with evil friends.
Which three?

Lack of shame, lack of dread of blame, and negligence—one who has not abandoned these three qualities is incapable of abandoning disrespect, difficult speech, and association with evil friends. Why is that? NidSa 25.13. Because:
One who lacks a sense of shame and lacks dread of blame becomes heedless; being heedless, he becomes disrespectful;
being disrespectful, he comes to have evil friends.
That evil friend, being thus, becomes one who is intent on finding fault; being intent on finding fault, he becomes faithless;
being faithless, he becomes [one who is]... [corrupt/fragmentary].
Being thus equal [to them], he becomes one of immoral conduct;
he desires restlessness;
he possesses forgetfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and distraction; and his mind becomes sluggish.
With a mind that has become sluggish, he settles into doubt and the view of a self-identity;
he clings to rules and observances;
and, his longing not having been crossed over, he remains possessed of passion, hatred, and delusion.
One who has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion is incapable of escaping sickness, old age, and death.
However, by abandoning three things, one is capable of abandoning sickness, old age, and death.
Which three?
Having abandoned these three factors— lust, hatred, and delusion— one is capable of abandoning sickness, old age, and death.
But having abandoned three other factors, one is capable of abandoning lust, hatred, and delusion.
Which three?
The view of a self-identity, the adherence to rites and rituals, and doubt.
Having abandoned these three factors, one is capable of abandoning passion, hatred, and delusion.

NidSa 25.16: However, by abandoning three factors, one is capable of abandoning the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Which three?
Improper mental attention (*ayoniśo manasikāra*), following a wrong path (*kumārgasevanā*), and a depressed mind (*līnacittatā*).

Having abandoned these three qualities, one is capable of abandoning the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
But having abandoned three other qualities, one is capable of abandoning improper mental attention (*ayoniśo manasikāra*), following wrong paths, and a depressed mind.
Which three?
Losing mindfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and distraction—
having abandoned these three factors, one is capable of abandoning improper mental attention, following wrong paths, and a sunken mind.
